passage: Last week, Karthik and I argued about whether the class plant needed more water. I said yes, he said no. When he showed me the soil was still damp, I felt hot in the face. I said, “Okay, you're right.” It was hard. Then I added, “But it still looks droopy, so maybe we check the sun.” Miss Suvarna smiled. Later Karthik said, “Thanks for listening.” I thought that conceding would feel like losing, but it felt more like working things out together. I'm Asif, and I still like being right, but I like plants growing better.

qa.q: What did Asif and Karthik argue about?
qa.a: Whether the class plant needed more water.

qa.q: How did Asif feel on seeing the damp soil, and how do you know?
qa.a: Asif felt embarrassed or stung about being wrong, since his face went hot and conceding was hard.

qa.q: What did Asif do that turned the argument into teamwork?
qa.a: Asif conceded with “Okay, you're right” and then added a new idea about checking the sun.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when Asif conceded?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt respected and relieved, since he thanked Asif for listening.

grounding: A child concedes with okay you're right and qualifies with but, and learns conceding is not losing.

passage: Observation note, Class 6. During the debate on school uniform, Sarika argued that uniforms should be worn every day. A classmate, Lavanya, made a strong point about comfort in hot weather. Sarika paused for a moment and said, “Okay, you're right about the heat. But maybe we can keep uniforms and choose lighter cloth?” The room got quiet, then some students nodded. I praised her for saying so gracefully. Afterwards she told me she felt a little sad, as if she'd lost something. I explained that changing her mind is thinking, not losing. She thought about that. Mr. Menon.

qa.q: What was the debate about?
qa.a: School uniform.

qa.q: What did Sarika feel after conceding the point?
qa.a: She felt a little sad, as if she had lost something, though she was open to hearing that changing her mind is not losing.

qa.q: What did Sarika's qualifying sentence add?
qa.a: She kept part of her view and offered a new idea about lighter cloth, so the class could work on a middle way.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have felt when Sarika conceded?
qa.a: Lavanya probably felt heard and pleased that her point about the heat was taken seriously.

grounding: A child concedes a point and qualifies it with but, and an adult praises conceding gracefully and says it is not losing.

passage: Wednesday. Irfan's diary. Today Disha and I argued at lunch about whether a spider is an insect. I said yes, obviously, it's a creepy-crawly. She said no, insects have six legs and spiders have eight. I got louder. She got the science book out and showed me. Eight legs. Two body parts, not three. My face went hot, and I wanted to say the book was old. But I said, “Okay. You're right. Spiders aren't insects.” Then I added, “But they're still creepy-crawlies.” She laughed and said, “Yes, fine, that's true.” At home Abbu said conceding like that is harder than winning. It didn't feel like losing, actually.

qa.q: How many legs does a spider have, according to the book?
qa.a: According to the book, spiders have eight legs.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when the book proved Disha right?
qa.a: Irfan felt embarrassed, face hot, and was tempted to argue the book was old.

qa.q: What did Irfan's “okay, you're right… but” achieve?
qa.a: It conceded the fact gracefully while keeping a fair point, so the argument ended with both of them laughing.

qa.q: How did Disha respond to Irfan's concession?
qa.a: Disha laughed and agreed spiders are still creepy-crawlies, meeting Irfan halfway.

grounding: Shows a child conceding a point gracefully and qualifying it, and an adult praising it so it doesn't feel like losing.

passage: On the dusty path to the Tuesday haat, Ritu and Sarika argued about which way was shorter. “Along the canal is quicker,” said Sarika. “No, through the mustard fields,” said Ritu. They raced, one each way. Sarika was already at the bangle stall, grinning, when Ritu arrived, panting. Ritu wanted to say Sarika had cheated. Instead she wiped her face and said, “Okay, the canal is shorter. But the field way has shade, and I'm not melting like you.” Sarika looked at her own red face and laughed. “Fair. Canal to come, fields to go back?” Ritu's grandmother, bargaining for onions nearby, nodded. “Well argued, both of you.”

qa.q: Where was Sarika when Ritu arrived?
qa.a: Sarika was already at the bangle stall.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she arrived panting?
qa.a: Ritu felt disappointed at losing and briefly tempted to accuse Sarika of cheating.

qa.q: How did Ritu's “Okay, but” turn the argument into a plan?
qa.a: By conceding the canal was shorter and adding that the fields have shade, she kept her point and led to a fair plan for both paths.

qa.q: How did Ritu's grandmother view the argument?
qa.a: She approved, saying both girls argued well, since they settled it fairly.

grounding: Shows a child conceding a point with okay, you're right and qualifying with but, and an adult praising the graceful concession.

passage: In their group project in a Vancouver classroom, Dalia and Mei couldn't agree on the poster layout. Dalia wanted the title at the bottom, big and bold. Mei wanted it at the top. “Nobody reads the bottom first,” Mei said. Dalia opened her mouth to argue, then looked at the other groups' posters on the wall. Every title was at the top, and she had read them first. “Okay,” she said slowly. “You're right about the top.” Then she added, “But can it be in my dark green? It stands out more.” Mei held the green pen up against the paper. “Yes. It does.” Their teacher, passing, said, “That's what good teamwork sounds like.”

qa.q: What colour did Dalia want the title in?
qa.a: Dalia wanted it in her dark green.

qa.q: What was Dalia feeling as she looked at the other posters?
qa.a: Dalia felt a little reluctant at first, then convinced as she saw every title at the top.

qa.q: Why did the teacher praise the way they settled it?
qa.a: Dalia conceded gracefully and added a fair qualification, so both ideas made the poster better without anyone feeling they lost.

qa.q: How did Mei respond to Dalia's suggestion about colour?
qa.a: Mei tested the green pen against the paper and agreed it stood out more.

grounding: Shows a child conceding a point and qualifying it with a yes, but, and an adult praising graceful conceding.

passage:
In the eco-club room, Sharmila had drawn the compost pit behind the canteen, with arrows and everything. Divyansh tapped the map. "But the vegetable garden's on the other side. We'd carry compost all the way across the ground every week."

Sharmila opened her mouth to argue, then looked at the map again. "Okay. You're right about the walk." She swallowed. "But if it's next to the garden, it's also next to Class 3's windows. The smell…"

Divyansh nodded slowly. "Yes, but we could put it in the far corner, by the wall."

Mr Thomas, the club teacher, grinned. "That's how good planning works. Sharmila, conceding a point takes guts. You didn't lose; the plan got better." Sharmila's shoulders came down from her ears.

qa.q: Where had Sharmila drawn the compost pit?
qa.a: Behind the canteen.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling as she said, "You're right about the walk"?
qa.a: A bit reluctant and tense, as her swallow and raised shoulders show, as if conceding meant losing; afterwards she relaxed.

qa.q: How did Mr Thomas help Sharmila not see conceding as losing?
qa.a: He praised her for conceding and pointed out that the plan got better, rather than naming a winner.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see Sharmila's "but" about the smell?
qa.a: Divyansh takes it as a fair point and builds on it with the far-corner idea, not as an attack.

grounding: It shows a child conceding a point and qualifying another with yes-but, and a teacher helping her see conceding as improving the plan, not losing.
